Eleven hybrid saunas, $6,999 to $18,999, median $8,995. A hybrid runs both heat sources in one cabin: a traditional stove for steam and high heat, and infrared panels for a lower-temperature session. You are paying for two systems in one room, which is why the floor here is $7,000 rather than the $3,000 an infrared-only cabin starts at.

The trade-off nobody states

Two heaters means two sets of running costs, two things to service and a cabin built to tolerate both. Six of the eleven publish a maximum temperature, and those six span 132°F to 190°F, which is the whole point: the same room does a 140°F infrared session and a 190°F traditional one. Eight publish a capacity, from two to six people.

Six of the eleven also fit red light panels — a third system in the same cabin, and worth asking what it adds over the infrared you are already paying for.

Power and delivery

Electrical requirements vary by model here and the listings are inconsistent about stating them, so treat the spec sheet for your exact unit as the answer and get it before you order. A stove-and-panel cabin at this size will generally need a dedicated 240V circuit installed by a licensed electrician.

Free shipping to the lower 48, no minimum, and it stops at the curb. Getting it inside is a $600 white-glove upgrade; inside and assembled is $1,800, which covers everything except the electrical work.

A hybrid needs the 240V circuit, so get the install quote first — the true total cost of a home sauna sets out what to ask.

Nine of the eleven are Golden Designs builds and two are Finnmark. If you only want one heat source, compare infrared saunas and traditional saunas first.
